episode_title: How can you make on-farm change easier?
question: Why did the hog industry collapse in Prince Edward Island during the 1990s?
transcript_excerpt: In the 1990s, the hog industry in Atlantic Canada collapsed when two packers in the region closed, leaving nowhere to send the hogs. This occurred at a time when the cost of production had risen significantly, and the industry contracted quite dramatically. Mark Sherman's family, like many others, did not have their cost of production at levels needed to survive this market shock.

episode_title: How can you make on-farm change easier?
question: How did Mark Sherman rebuild his family farm after returning to Prince Edward Island in 2008?
transcript_excerpt: After buying back the family farm in 2008, Sherman maintained a full-time off-farm job initially to pay bills while building the greenhouse business, knowing he could earn more elsewhere than from the farm in early years. He started with a 0.6-acre greenhouse and gradually added efficiencies and lights over a couple of years before beginning expansion in 2015, allowing the business to grow only once it generated enough revenue to support him full-time.

episode_title: How can you make on-farm change easier?
question: What did Mark Sherman learn from working in Mexico that he brought back to his greenhouse business on Prince Edward Island?
transcript_excerpt: In Mexico, Sherman worked in a 25-acre greenhouse operation after leaving a 0.6-acre greenhouse in PEI, which taught him how to manage scale differently and provided intellectual, social, and management-level learning. He also gained networks and connections—some of which he maintains to today—and learned what practices not to implement based on seeing regulatory and safety gaps in other countries. These people connections enabled him to bring skilled workers back to his farm.

episode_title: How can you make on-farm change easier?
question: What are the three key characteristics that separate farming businesses able to adapt from those that struggle with change?
transcript_excerpt: The businesses genuinely good at change had three things in common: clarity of decision-making, a license to experiment and fail, and somewhere to put what they learned. None of these are technical—you cannot get a diploma in any of them—they are all about behavior, not knowledge or expertise.

episode_title: How can you make on-farm change easier?
question: What four habits did Peter Green identify as most common among farming businesses that make change consistently?
transcript_excerpt: The four habits are: making change part of the annual rhythm of the business rather than something forced; running small safe-to-fail trials rather than betting everything on one massive transformational shift; deciding in advance when a trial should stop with stop-loss discipline; and recording what the business learned so that learning survives beyond a single season.
